doc.title: Branford Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Folk music in composers' work and Villa-Lobos
summary: Composers from Bach to Mahler drew on folk traditions; he comments on Villa-Lobos studying with Milhaud.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: There were many composers that were influenced by the jazz tradition, the music coming out of America. Ravel and of course you’ve done Milhaud. You also seem to…You toured with the Brazilian ensemble, so Villa-Lobos must figure pretty large…
I like his music. He was very prolific and he wrote a lot. A lot. A lot.
And really dealt with the folk elements in his country.
Well, they all did. They all did.
Yeah, too a greater, or lesser extent.

They all did. [You know…] It comes out of the folk music. It’s not detached from …. Well, twentieth-century music, a lot of that is detached from the people. But, before that, whether you’re talking about Bach, or Mozart, all this music Bach has this … he did an entire rearrangement of old traditional Christian songs. They are finding all this stuff that he did. Songs by other people that he just reharmonized and added …and they have. I have the record right now. There is so much folk music in Mozart’s music. There is so much folk music in Beethoven’s music. Mahler, he had the regular German folk tradition, and the Jewish folk tradition in there. You could take certain parts of Mahler songs and you could turn them into klezmer tunes in two seconds.
Shoot, Mahler was checking out Chinese.
Hey, you know, why not? You check it all out.

You check it all out. [But, yeah…I mean…you know…] I don’t think that [you know that] Villa-Lobos had the lock on it because [you know] he studied with Milhaud. And he went to Paris and he studied. And you hear a lot of that French influence in – in his writing. [But, ah…] I think that the one thing that Milhaud did that was really great is that he didn’t try to recreate jazz in his writing. ‘Cause all the guys that used jazz as an influence, it was always about “Yat-ta-ta-ta-taa.” “Ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-taa.
